reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: The most severe of the female X-polysomies, carrying three extra X chromosomes
Moderate-to-severe intellectual disability is typical and more marked than in triple X
Short stature is characteristic, in contrast to the tall stature of triple X, reflecting the escalating dosage effect at higher polysomies
Characteristic facial features include upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, and coarse features that may superficially resemble Down syndrome
Congenital heart defects, notably patent ductus arteriosus and septal defects, are common
Skeletal anomalies include radioulnar synostosis, joint laxity or contractures, and clinodactyly
Microcephaly, recurrent infections, and ovarian and uterine hypoplasia with delayed or absent puberty are frequent
reference.pathophysiology: Pentasomy X arises from sequential non-disjunction during maternal meiosis, producing an egg with four X chromosomes and thus a 49,XXXXX conceptus. Although all but one X is inactivated, the burden of genes that escape X-inactivation rises with each additional X, so gene-dosage effects are amplified relative to trisomy X. This escalating imbalance explains why pentasomy X is far more severe, with pronounced intellectual disability, short stature, congenital malformations, and dysmorphism, illustrating the general rule that each additional sex chromosome worsens the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Down syndrome, given the overlapping facial features
Other polysomy X or Y syndromes
Syndromic intellectual disability of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey, including the forearm for radioulnar synostosis
Endocrine and pubertal assessment with pelvic imaging for uterine and ovarian development
redFlags: Failure to progress through puberty requiring endocrine input
reference.prognosis: Guarded; most individuals have significant intellectual disability and need lifelong support, with outcome influenced by cardiac and other malformations, although survival into adulthood occurs.
pitfalls: Mistaking the facial features for Down syndrome and not performing a karyotype
Expecting tall stature, as in triple X, when short stature is typical
Missing congenital heart disease or radioulnar synostosis
Underestimating the degree of intellectual disability compared with lower-grade X-polysomies
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
